question: How should a practitioner frame an ML problem, move a prototype to production, test it, and keep learning after the book's algorithms are known?

results.claim: Worked example: a perfect fraud model that saves $100 a month is not worth starting; tens of thousands of dollars a month might be.
results.setup: Fraud detection scoping thought experiment: ask 'What if I built the perfect model?'
results.quote:
If perfectly detecting any fraud will save your company $100
a month, these possible savings will probably not be enough to warrant the effort of
you even starting to develop an algorithm.
results.where: Approaching a Machine Learning Problem, p. 358

results.claim: Even automating a small share of decisions (10 percent) while routing the rest to humans can cut response time or cost.
results.setup: Human-in-the-loop design; no data given, an illustrative range of 90, 50 or 10 percent.
results.quote:
But if an algorithm can make 90 percent, 50 percent, or maybe even
just 10 percent of decisions automatically, that might already increase response time
or reduce cost.

limits: No experiments or data; advice is the authors' judgement with no evidence offered.

Dated: written around 2016 (mentions AlphaGo, mllib on Spark/Hadoop, vowpal wabbit as current); neural networks are given a single paragraph and the authors say any state-of-the-art reference 'will soon be outdated'.
Online testing gets one paragraph: A/B testing is described but no sample size, duration, significance test or guardrail metrics.
Build-vs-buy is touched only as 'reimplement in a production language vs embed Python/scikit-learn' and 'build your own estimator'; no cost or decision criteria.
practices: Before choosing an algorithm, decide what question you are asking (exploratory vs goal-driven) and how to define and measure success (p. 357).
Ask how you will measure that the model works, whether you have data to evaluate it, and what the business impact would be if it succeeds (p. 358).
Prefer measuring with a business metric (profit, losses) where possible; otherwise bound the value by asking what a perfect model would be worth (p. 358).
Treat modelling as one loop with data collection, cleaning and error analysis; collecting more or different data or reformulating the task may pay off more than endless grid searches (p. 358).
Decide whether to put humans in the loop: let the algorithm handle simple cases and reroute uncertain or complicated ones to a person, depending on whether decisions must be immediate (p. 358).

Analytics teams may prototype in Python or R while production teams use Go, Scala, C++ or Java; a common fix is to reimplement the found solution in the production framework rather than embed the library (p. 359).

In production weigh reliability, predictability, runtime and memory; keep it simple, and for each pipeline step ask what complexity it adds, how robust it is to data and infrastructure change, and whether its benefit warrants that (p. 359).
Read Sculley et al.-style 'Machine Learning: The High Interest Credit Card of Technical Debt' (cited as by Google researchers) for the maintenance trade-offs of production ML (p. 359).

After offline evaluation on a held-out test set, run online/live tests; A/B testing exposes a portion of users to algorithm A and the rest to B, records success metrics for a set period, then selects by those metrics. Often A is the new model and B the established system (pp. 359-360).
Consider bandit algorithms as a more elaborate form of online testing (p. 360).

If preprocessing is data dependent, wrap it in a custom scikit-learn estimator (BaseEstimator plus TransformerMixin, ClassifierMixin or RegressorMixin) so it stays inside Pipeline, GridSearchCV and cross_val_score and so inside the cross-validation loop (pp. 360-361).
Choose tools by need: statsmodels for statistical inference rather than prediction, R for statistics and visualisation, vowpal wabbit for large or streaming data, Spark MLlib for clusters (p. 362).
If the problem has known structure (e.g. maps plus GPS, accelerometer, compass), express it in a probabilistic model, using PyMC or Stan, instead of a black box (pp. 363-364).

Scale in this order: more RAM or a rented machine first, since most datasets are small; then out-of-core learning; then a cluster (Spark) only when infrastructure exists; vw is an alternative with distributed features (pp. 364-365).
Practice on competitions (Kaggle) and OpenML, but remember they fix the metric and data; defining the problem and collecting data matter more than the last percent of accuracy (pp. 365-366).
